title: Hotchkiss Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Hotchkiss wells have a 90 ft median depth, 15 gpm median yield, and estimated finished costs of $10,500-$18,800.
h1: Hotchkiss, Colorado Well Depth, Yield, and Cost
intro_html:
Buying land near Hotchkiss means dealing with a generally shallow, productive well area, but the records still show meaningful variation. Among permitted wells within five miles of Hotchkiss, the median reported depth is 90 feet and the median reported yield is 15 gallons per minute. Those figures come from different parts of the permit record: 383 wells report depth, while 126 report pump yield.

Most permits identify an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with alluvial and Mancos wells appearing rarely. The local record includes domestic, stock, irrigation, and monitoring wells, so a nearby well is useful evidence but not a guarantee for a new lot.

sections.heading: Hotchkiss well depth: shallow is common, but not guaranteed
sections.html:
Hotchkiss wells have a median reported depth of 90 feet. The middle half runs from 40 to 139 feet, which is the most useful range for an initial drilling discussion. Fifty-six percent of the recorded wells are under 100 feet, and 40% fall between 100 and 300 feet. Only 2% are between 300 and 600 feet, while 1% are deeper than 600 feet.

The deepest recorded well reaches 1,386 feet, so shallow ground should not be treated as a promise. Mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground can change across a short distance. Fractured-bedrock wells can also be unpredictable because water may depend on individual fractures rather than a consistent layer. A driller's bid should clearly state the assumed depth, casing, grout, and what happens if the hole must go deeper.

sections.heading: What a Hotchkiss well may produce
sections.html:
The reported yield picture is favorable, though only 126 wells include a pump-yield record. The median is 15.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 12.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-six percent of reported wells produce more than 15 gallons per minute. Another 26% fall between 5 and 15 gallons per minute.

Low-yield wells still occur. Seven percent report 1 to 5 gallons per minute, and 1% report under 1 gallon per minute. For a household buyer, that makes the actual well test, recovery behavior, storage, and permitted use more important than the area median alone. A domestic permit is not the same as a guarantee of irrigation supply, and an existing stock or irrigation well may not compare directly with a household well.

sections.heading: Water levels around Hotchkiss and the apparent trend
sections.html:
Among the 47 wells reporting a static water level, the median depth to water is 12 feet below the surface. The middle half ranges from 3 to 40 feet. That shallow median can reduce pumping lift, but water levels vary with location, season, well construction, and measurement conditions.

The decade figures deserve attention. The median static water level was 3 feet below surface in the 2010s and 32 feet in the 2020s. That is a deeper reported water level in the newer decade, but the records do not establish the cause or prove a uniform regional decline. The sample is limited, and the wells measured in each decade may differ. Before buying, ask for the original well construction report and recent pumping or static-level information.

sections.heading: Who has drilled near Hotchkiss, and when
sections.html:
Permit activity stretches across several generations. Records show 2 permits from the 1950s, 3 from the 1960s, 47 from the 1970s, 26 from the 1980s, 133 from the 1990s, 187 from the 2000s, 79 from the 2010s, and 47 from the 2020s. The newest permit year is 2025. That history gives a buyer a useful way to compare older wells with newer construction.

Wildcat Drilling & Pump, Inc. (Kissner, Billy D.) appears on 109 records. Bill Kissner Drilling Inc (Kissner, Bill F.) appears on 86, and Authorized (Pe, Pg) appears on 40. These records identify past permit activity, not a recommendation or proof of current availability. Check the DWR permit and construction records for the specific parcel, then confirm licensing, scope, and pricing directly before hiring.

sections.heading: Estimated cost to drill a well in Hotchkiss
sections.html:
For the mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground reported around Hotchkiss, the drilling model uses a typical rate of $50 to $75 per foot. At the 90-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at about $4,500 to $6,800. That is not the complete water-system price.

A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $10,500 to $18,800 at the median depth. A deep hole, difficult access, extra casing, or an unsuccessful drilling attempt can change the final bill. Ask for a written bid separating drilling, casing and grout, pump equipment, trenching, electrical, testing, and permit-related work. Compare the bid with nearby construction reports rather than relying only on the countywide or five-mile median.

sections.heading: Hotchkiss risks to check before you build
sections.html:
Well quantity is only one part of due diligence. Mapped environmental records within about ten miles include 16 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 19 historic mine features, and 11 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those locations do not prove contamination at a particular parcel, but they are reasons to check the well location, groundwater direction, past land use, and available laboratory results.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible even in a productive area. Confirm the permit status, construction report, casing and grout, pump test, water quality, and static level. Septic placement also matters: keep the well and septic system separated according to the applicable county and state requirements, and verify that the lot has suitable soil, setbacks, access, and room for a replacement system before finalizing a building plan.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Hotchkiss lot
sections.html:
Start with the parcel's own DWR permit history, then inspect neighboring wells in Hotchkiss, Lazear, Paonia, Crawford, Cedaredge, Orchard City, and Somerset only as local context. Nearby records can show likely depth and construction conditions, but they cannot establish the yield or water quality of an unbuilt well.

For an existing home, make the sale contingent on reviewing the well permit, construction report, pump performance, water test, storage equipment, and any known water-level history. For vacant land, price the project using the local drilling range and keep a contingency for deeper drilling or a dry hole. Also confirm household-use rights, septic feasibility, driveway access, electric service, and any augmentation-plan issue before committing to a home design or irrigation expectation.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Hotchkiss, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Hotchkiss is 90 feet. The middle half runs from 40 to 139 feet, and 56% of recorded wells are under 100 feet. Depth still varies substantially: the deepest record is 1,386 feet. A nearby well helps set expectations, but the parcel's geology and the driller's construction report matter more than the median alone.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Hotchkiss?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $50 to $75 per foot. At the 90-foot median depth, the drilled hole is estimated at $4,500 to $6,800. A finished system with pump, tank, trenching, and electrical is estimated at $10,500 to $18,800. Access, casing, deeper drilling, and difficult ground can increase the final price.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Hotchkiss?
faq.a: Among the 126 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 15.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 12.0 to 15.0 gallons per minute. Sixty-six percent report more than 15 gallons per minute. Low-yield wells still occur: 7% report 1 to 5 gallons per minute and 1% report under 1 gallon per minute.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Hotchkiss?
faq.a: The permit records do not establish drinking-water safety for a particular property. Within about ten miles, mapped records include 16 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 19 historic mine features, and 11 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test an existing or new well through a qualified laboratory and review nearby land uses before relying on it for household water.

faq.q: Has the water table dropped near Hotchkiss?
faq.a: Reported static water levels were a median of 3 feet below surface in the 2010s and 32 feet in the 2020s. That shows deeper measurements in the newer decade, but only 47 wells report static levels, and the measured wells and conditions may differ. The figures suggest a question to investigate, not proof of a uniform regional decline.
